style: Use case: historical-scene. Asset: one bespoke HadithCritic editorial thumbnail. Render a single landscape image at 1536 x 1024 pixels, 3:2 aspect ratio. Exquisite antique copperplate engraving and etching, dense precise fine crosshatching and stippling, coherent sepia-brown ink on pale warm aged parchment (#e5d7bd), subtle paper grain. Match the existing archival scholarly engravings, not a modern painting, photo or cartoon. Scene occupies center and right; leftmost 20 percent gently fades into almost empty parchment, full bleed, no frame. Strong readable main subject at thumbnail scale, restrained antique gold details. No lettering, text, pseudo-writing, labels, numbers, logos, watermarks, UI, or typography. No depiction of Muhammad, other named prophets, or God. This is a conceptual editorial illustration of the article's subject, not documentary evidence.

assets.alt: A lone visitor approaches a leather campaign tent at Tabūk, with six stones along the path and a frontier encampment beyond.
assets.scene: Article 32: The Six Signs Hadith, a private report in a leather tent at Tabuk later expanded into Syrian apocalyptic predictions. Show a weathered domed leather campaign tent in a rocky Arabian frontier encampment, its dark entrance slightly open, a lone cloaked visitor seen from behind approaching it, six small plain stones aligned along the path in the right foreground as a quiet visual motif for the six signs. Distant low hills, a few sparse camp banners and date palms. No visible person inside the tent. The private tent encounter is the unmistakable focus, not a generic library or grand mosque.

assets.alt: Four plain empty seats lead toward a raised ornate throne, with counting pebbles marking the transition from caliphate to kingship.
assets.scene: Article 33: the thirty-year caliphate report, a retrospective calculation legitimating four caliphs and drawing a boundary before Umayyad kingship. In an early Islamic stone assembly courtyard, four plain unoccupied low wooden chairs stand in a receding row; beyond them at right a single larger richly carved empty royal throne stands elevated on steps under an architectural arch. In the near foreground a small counting board with groups of pebbles and a reed stylus suggests retrospective arithmetic without numerals. The sharp transition from modest assembly chairs to raised dynastic throne is the main image. Distant Syrian courtyard and geometric stonework. No crowns on the four chairs, no identifiable historical rulers, no chess pieces, no modern furniture.

assets.alt: A winding Arabian mountain path disappears into cloud beyond a clear foreground, illustrating the limits of knowledge of the unseen.
assets.scene: Article 34: The Prophet Did Not Know the Future, Quranic distinction between specific revealed disclosures and possession of the unseen. An expansive rocky Arabian mountain pass, a clearly illuminated path and simple way marker in the foreground, then the path turns sharply and disappears completely into a thick bank of finely stippled mist behind the ridge. A small unoccupied travel shelter and waterskin beside the visible section of path give a human scale. The hidden horizon is the dominant metaphor. Light only illuminates the near ground; the far destination remains unknowable. No fortune teller, crystal ball, clock, supernatural character or prophet depiction. A distinctive contemplative landscape rather than a book still life.

assets.alt: Early medieval siege tents and a commander overlook Constantinople’s land walls and Byzantine skyline.
assets.scene: Article 35: Constantinople conquest hadith and Maslama's early eighth-century Umayyad siege context. Show the massive triple Theodosian land walls of Byzantine Constantinople across the right middle distance; beyond them the silhouette of Hagia Sophia in its Byzantine form without minarets. In foreground an early eighth-century Arab campaign commander, seen from behind in practical cloak and simple helmet, studies the defended city from beside leather tents, spear standards and a wooden siege ladder. A few galleys on distant water. No Ottoman cannons, Ottoman crescent flags, fifteenth-century uniforms, explosions, gore or triumphal entry. The siege context, not a generic Islamic city, must be unmistakable.

assets.alt: Two scholars compare contrasting manuscript leaves while ordinary worshippers pray in a courtyard beyond.
assets.scene: Article 36: point-by-point refutation of hadith apologetics, competing Quran readings, preservation, consensus and the claim that ritual depends on hadith books. An early Islamic study courtyard seen obliquely: two scholars in plain robes sit opposite each other at a low table comparing two unlettered parchment leaves, one gestures toward a small group quietly praying together in the distant courtyard while the other points to a closed compilation. A reed stylus separates the parallel leaves. Depict reasoned examination of claims and the relationship between inherited practice and written scholarship. No argument caricature, angry faces, screens, microphones, modern video interface, actual Arabic writing or text. Make the live prayer scene clearly visible behind the comparison.

assets.alt: An elderly recitation teacher listens to pupils beside seven manuscript bundles, illustrating the human transmission of canonical readings.
assets.scene: Article 37: Fallible Transmitters Transmitting Infallible Text, Ibn Mujahid's seven readings and the memory limitations of human reciters. An elderly Quran recitation instructor sits attentively in a modest early medieval teaching alcove, students with differing loose parchment leaves sit in a half circle. On a low shelf or table behind him exactly seven modest manuscript bundles stand separately, each tied with plain cord and without text, visually representing the seven canonical reading traditions. The teacher and a pupil compare leaves, with humane dignified treatment of age, no disability caricature. Simple Iraqi brick arches, reed mats. The focus is human listening, correction, and seven selected readings, not an anonymous book pile.

assets.alt: A citron, dates, aromatic branches and a bitter colocynth lie between two manuscript traditions, illustrating the shared fruit parable.
assets.scene: Article 38: The Parable of the Believer and the Citron, comparison of Vayikra Rabbah and the hadith fruit taxonomy. A large botanically recognizable bumpy oblong citron dominates a carved stone tabletop at right, beside a small bunch of dates, sprigs of sweet basil and myrtle, a willow twig and a small round striped colocynth bitter gourd. Behind this botanical set, two modest open manuscript forms face one another, a rolled two-rod scroll and a stitched early Islamic codex, both with completely blank surfaces. A subtle Basran courtyard garden beyond. The distinctive citron and contrasting taste/fragrance plants are the focus; the two manuscript traditions indicate comparison. No lemon substituted for citron, no invented Hebrew or Arabic, no religious caricatures or modern labels.

assets.alt: A woman pauses at the threshold of a prayer space, with an unused woven prayer mat inside.
assets.scene: Article 39: Hisham ibn Urwa and the reports barring menstruating women from prayer. A dignified adult woman in modest early Islamic clothing, seen in three-quarter back view, stands quietly just outside the open threshold of a simple domestic prayer room; an unused woven prayer mat lies inside aligned toward a plain niche, a clay water jug beside it. No guard physically bars her, no blood or anatomy. Her hand rests at the doorway as if weighing an imposed restriction. A small closed legal parchment bundle on a nearby ledge is secondary. The subject is exclusion from worship and loss of prayers, conveyed respectfully without a fantasy event. No modern mosque decor, no readable text.

assets.alt: A night watchman catches a cloaked thief taking grain from Ramadan zakāt sacks in a lamplit storeroom.
assets.scene: Article 40: Abu Hurairah's nocturnal zakat thief narrative, the thief repeatedly steals Ramadan food provisions and finally teaches a protective recitation. Inside a simple seventh-century grain storeroom at night, a watchman in plain robes holds the wrist of a furtive cloaked adult reaching into an open sack of grain; other tied food sacks and woven baskets sit behind. One oil lamp creates dramatic engraved shadow, spilled grain on the floor is clearly visible. The thief is outwardly human and anonymous, his face mostly in shadow; no horned monster, magic smoke or literal supernatural creature. No prophet depicted, no violence. Strong foreground focus on grain theft and the caught hand.

assets.alt: A comb, date-palm spathe and knotted cord rest beside a stone well, recalling the bewitchment report’s competing recensions.
assets.scene: Article 41: al-Amash and Hisham ibn Urwa's competing bewitchment reports. A modest stone well in an early Medinan date-palm courtyard, its rope and bucket pulled up onto the rim. In the right foreground a wooden comb, loose fine hair-like fibers, a dried male date-palm spathe and a short cord with several knots are carefully laid on stone beside two separate blank manuscript leaves, suggesting comparison of the detailed family dossier and shorter knot report. The physical well and retrieved objects are the focus. No magical glow, occult symbols, pentagrams, stereotyped Jewish sorcerer, prophet, suffering person or invented writing. A restrained evidence still life rooted in the report's specific objects.

assets.alt: A robed person offers water to a thirsty animal beside a birdbath, evoking the shared teaching of mercy toward God’s creatures.
assets.scene: Article 42: Being Merciful to the Inhabitants of Earth, parallel compassion teaching in hadith and Tractate Shabbat. A robed person bends to offer a shallow clay bowl of water to a thirsty stray dog in an early Middle Eastern courtyard; small birds drink from a second stone water basin nearby. Behind the scene, a two-rod scroll and a simple stitched manuscript rest side by side on a ledge, both unlettered and secondary, indicating the two wisdom traditions. The act of care for living creatures must dominate, compassionate and quiet. No deity in clouds, no halos, no modern symbols or religious caricature, no text. Warm sepia but exact engraving style.

assets.alt: A traveller retrieves a wandering camel by its trailing reins near a Tabūk encampment, with a distant funeral gathering suggesting the keeper-of-secrets narrative.
assets.scene: Article 43: Hudhayfah as keeper of secrets, the Tabuk camel retrieval story and later funeral attendance as a signal of hidden identities. In rocky Arabian terrain at dusk an anonymous traveller in plain cloak catches the long trailing reins of a wandering saddled camel beside a modest expedition camp. The camel and reins dominate the right foreground. In far background a small group of distant figures stands around a plainly shrouded bier outside a settlement, with one figure waiting apart; subtle distant vignette recalling the later funeral story, not a dramatic death scene. No identifiable prophet, no corpse details, no secret-name scroll or invented text, no fantasy spy imagery. Keep camel anatomically correct.

assets.alt: A chained scholar faces a court scribe and an official demanding a written recantation, with a whip laid on the table.
assets.scene: Article 44: Flogging, Torture and Transmission of Hadith, caliphal coercion and forced recantation. An early Abbasid court chamber: a dignified detained scholar fully clothed sits at right with a loose iron shackle at his ankle, while a court scribe presents a blank recantation parchment and reed pen; a standing official watches from beside an elevated empty seat. A coiled plain leather whip lies conspicuously on the low table, unused. A barred doorway and guard remain in shadow. Focus on pressure to change scholarly testimony and the threat shaping the archive. No active flogging, wounds, blood, nudity or graphic torture. Strong restrained power imbalance, not generic library imagery.

assets.alt: A traveller leaves through a city gate while a jurist examines an apostasy ruling beside a sheathed sword and prison doorway.
assets.scene: Article 45: Ikrima, the apostasy execution report and later legal guardrails of imprisonment, bread and repentance. A traveller seen from behind steps toward an open early Arabian city gate, representing departure from the community. At right foreground a seated legal transmitter considers an unlettered parchment, beside a plain straight sword resting safely in its scabbard. A small prison doorway nearby holds a clay water cup and a single loaf of bread on its threshold, evoking the later three-day repentance provision. Gate departure, legal threat and prison bread are distinct and readable, no execution, no injured body, no prophet or identifiable historical portrait, no modern religious iconography or writing.

assets.alt: A compiler compares several cord-linked manuscript bundles, with one excluded bundle set apart, illustrating selective Ibn ʿAbbās transmission in the Muwaṭṭaʾ.
assets.scene: Article 46: Ibn Abbas and Ikrima in Malik's Muwatta, distribution of transmission routes, dominant Zuhri channel and selective treatment of Ikrima. A seated early Medinan compiler at a low wooden desk studies a central open stitched codex with entirely blank leaves. Several small rolled report bundles on the right are linked by thin physical cords through one prominent brass ring into the codex; one single unconnected bundle is deliberately set aside on a separate stone ledge, representing the rarely admitted Ikrima material. Behind the desk an official waits at the courtyard door, a quiet suggestion of court connections, not a confrontation. Clear physical sorting and selective admission, no modern network diagram, no labels, no generic stack of books.

assets.alt: An intact recitation codex stands apart from divergent loose report leaves passed between scribes, illustrating the distinction between scripture and later narration.
assets.scene: Article 47: Hadith Cannot Logically Be Treated as Wahi, distinction between revealed recitation and later human reports transmitted by meaning. In an early Islamic scholarly courtyard a single carefully bound open recitation codex sits steady on a simple wooden support at center-right. Farther right, three anonymous scribes pass separate loose parchment leaves between them, with differing blank page shapes, folds and additions illustrating paraphrase and variant reports. A clean physical space separates the central bound codex from the scattered report leaves. No divine beam that endorses a theological claim, no deity or prophet, no labels, pseudo-Arabic or grade symbols. Make the contrast of fixed recitation and human transmission visually obvious while maintaining dignified scholarly engraving.

assets.alt: A compiler examines a single witness’s separate parchment fragments while officials burn earlier manuscript leaves in a courtyard brazier.
assets.scene: Article 48: False Verses Added into the Mushaf, singular testimony for the final two verses and Marwan's reported destruction of Hafsa's manuscript. An early Umayyad administrative courtyard. In the right foreground a compiler compares an open stitched codex with exactly two separate small parchment fragments supplied by a lone standing witness; all page surfaces are blank, no actual sacred verses or invented writing. Behind them an official places a bundle of older parchment leaves into a small stone brazier, with restrained flames and rising smoke, illustrating destruction of comparison evidence. No person being burned, no modern book burning crowd, no prophet. The single witness, two separate leaves and background manuscript destruction are the specific editorial motifs, not generic religious conflict.
